title: Unsolved Murder, Captive Wives, and a Body on a Tree
summary: Moses gives five laws about life, death, and family. A town nearest an unsolved killing must perform a rite to remove bloodguilt; a captive woman taken as a wife must be given time to mourn and may not be sold; a firstborn son keeps his double share even if his mother is unloved; a persistently rebellious son may be brought by both parents before the elders; and the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree must be buried the same day.
story: The laws of chapters 19 to 25 keep returning to one concern: that the land God is giving should not be defiled by innocent blood or by the breakdown of justice. Chapter 19 dealt with refuge for the accidental killer and chapter 20 with war. Chapter 21 moves from the battlefield into the household, and several of its laws follow directly on the war laws (the captive woman is taken in a campaign). The chapter keeps the reader inside ordinary Israelite life, where fields, marriages, inheritances, and difficult sons all fall under God's word. Its final law, about a body hung on a tree, became one of the most important Old Testament texts for the early church's understanding of the cross.
historical:
Every ancient society had to decide who was responsible when a body was found and no killer could be named. The Code of Hammurabi, from Babylon in about the eighteenth century BC, required the city and its governor to compensate the family when a robber was not caught and a victim was killed. Deuteronomy also makes the nearest town responsible, but the responsibility is before God: the town's elders must publicly deny guilt and ask the LORD to accept atonement for his people.

The hanging of verses 22-23 was not a method of execution. The body of someone already put to death was displayed on a tree or post as a public warning, and Joshua does this with the bodies of defeated Canaanite kings, taking them down at sunset (Joshua 8:29; 10:26-27). Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Temple Scroll discusses this law in connection with hanging a living person, which many scholars take to refer to crucifixion, the Roman method of execution. The same law lies behind the Gospel of John's note that the Jewish leaders asked for the bodies to be taken down before the Sabbath (John 19:31).
cultural:
Inheritance in Israel usually passed to sons, and the firstborn received a double share so that he could carry the responsibility of heading the family. Polygamy, though never commanded, was permitted and known, and the Genesis stories show its misery: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and favoritism between wives spilled into favoritism between sons. Verses 15-17 forbid a father from letting love for one wife override the rights of another wife's child.

The captive woman's shaved head, trimmed nails, and changed clothing marked a transition out of her old life and gave her a month to mourn her parents. In a world where women taken in war were routinely raped or sold as slaves, this law restrained the soldier: he must wait, he must marry her, and if he later rejects her she goes free and may not be sold. The rebellious son law places the judgment in the hands of the town elders rather than the father alone, and it requires both mother and father to bring the charge. A view recorded in the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 71a) held that the case of the stubborn and rebellious son had never actually been carried out, because the rabbis hedged it with so many conditions.
literary: The chapter is a collection of five case laws, each introduced by if or when and each concerned with a boundary between life and death or between a household and the community. The first and last laws frame the chapter around the land: blood that is not atoned for and a body left hanging both defile the land the LORD is giving. The elders' declaration in verses 7-8 is a short liturgy, a prayer spoken beside the stream over the heifer. The middle three laws concern family order and move from wife to firstborn to rebellious son. The refrain to purge the evil from among you appears again in verses 9 and 21.

outline.t: Marrying a woman taken captive in war
A hanged body buried the same day

doctrines.note: Bloodshed brings guilt on a community even when no one knows who did it, and it must be atoned for. The elders' prayer asks God to accept atonement for the people he has redeemed, showing that removal of guilt is his gift, not a human achievement.

The chapter protects the weaker members of a household: a captive wife who may not be sold, a son whose mother is unloved, and even a rebellious son, who cannot be punished by his father alone but must be brought before the elders by both parents.

The curse on one hung on a tree expresses God's judgment on sin publicly displayed. Yet the law also limits that display: the body must be buried before nightfall, so that even judgment does not become degradation.

words.note: Kipper, to atone or make atonement. The verb is used across the Old Testament for covering or wiping away guilt so that relationship with God is restored. Here it is used twice in verse 8: the elders ask God to accept atonement, and the text says the bloodshed will be atoned for.

Bekor, firstborn. The firstborn son held a special place in inheritance and in Israel's memory, since God had spared Israel's firstborn at the Passover and called Israel his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). Verse 17 calls him the firstfruits of his father's strength.

Sarar, to be stubborn or rebellious. The word describes persistent defiance rather than a single act of disobedience, which is why the case describes a son who does not listen even when disciplined. The prophets later use the same word for Israel's stubbornness toward God (Isaiah 1:23; Hosea 4:16).

Qelalah, curse. The opposite of blessing, it means the state of being under God's judgment or rejection. Verse 23 says one hung on a tree is under God's curse, a phrase the apostle Paul takes up to explain what happened at the cross.

christ: The last law of the chapter is directly used in the New Testament. Paul writes that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, and he cites this verse (Galatians 3:13). To a first-century Jew, a crucified man looked like someone rejected by God, which made the claim that Jesus was the Messiah seem impossible. Paul turns that objection into the heart of the gospel: Jesus did bear God's curse, and he bore it for others. Peter also speaks of the apostles' opponents killing Jesus by hanging him on a tree (Acts 5:30; 10:39), and Jesus' body was taken down and buried before nightfall. There may be a further echo in the rebellious son law, since Jesus was accused of being a glutton and a drunkard (Matthew 11:19), though the New Testament does not draw the connection itself. The unsolved murder rite, with atonement asked for a people God has redeemed, points more generally to the Bible's teaching that guilt must be dealt with by God himself.

hard.q: How can the law allow a rebellious son to be stoned, or a captive woman to be taken as a wife?
hard.a:
Both laws are painful to read, and it helps to see what they restrained as well as what they permitted. In many ancient societies a father held the power of life and death over his children. This law takes that power away from the father and gives it to the community's elders, requires both parents to agree, and limits the case to a son who is persistently defiant and destructive (a glutton and a drunkard, not a child who misbehaves once). Jewish interpreters narrowed it so far that, according to a view recorded in the Talmud, it was never applied.

The captive woman law likewise assumes the brutal reality of ancient warfare and then limits what a soldier may do: he must wait a month, he must marry her rather than use her, and she cannot be sold or enslaved if he rejects her. Many interpreters see these laws, like the laws on divorce that Jesus discusses in Matthew 19:8, as regulations given because of the hardness of human hearts, moving a violent world toward justice rather than describing God's ideal. Others stress that the laws already expressed real protection for the vulnerable in their setting. Readers can hold both: these texts are not a picture of perfection, but they are aimed at restraint.

questions: The elders of the nearest town had to take responsibility for a killing they did not commit. Where are you part of a community responsible for harm no one will own?
The law protected the son of an unloved wife from his father's favoritism. How does favoritism in families still shape children's lives?
Paul read the curse of one hung on a tree as the key to the cross. What does it mean to you that Christ became a curse for others?
